title: Resetting the Economy for the Ghana We Want
presented_by: Dr. Cassiel Ato Forson (MP), Minister for Finance, on the authority of H.E. John Dramani Mahama
source_note: All 'page' values are PDF page numbers of 2025-Budget-Statement-and-Economic-Policy.pdf (printed page number = PDF page - 12 in the main text). Money in GH¢ million unless stated.
headline_summary: The first budget of the Mahama administration frames 2025 as a 'reset' of an economy described as in severe distress, with 2024 marked by a primary deficit of 3.9% of GDP (vs a 0.5% surplus target), 23.8% inflation and GH¢67.5bn of arrears. It front-loads a spending-led fiscal adjustment of about 5.3 percentage points of GDP to reach a primary surplus of 1.5% of GDP, cutting primary spending from 19.8% to 14.6% of GDP while abolishing 'nuisance taxes' (E-Levy, betting tax, emissions levy) and raising the mining Growth & Sustainability Levy to 3%. It uncaps GETFund, NHIL and the Road Fund, funds a GH¢13.85bn 'Big Push' infrastructure programme, creates the Ghana Gold Board, and introduces social initiatives such as free first-year tertiary fees, free sanitary pads, MahamaCares and an expanded LEAP, within the IMF-supported programme.

debt.restructuring_notes: Restructuring ~93% complete: US$20.3bn domestic notes/bonds, US$13.1bn Eurobonds (37% nominal haircut ~US$5bn, ~US$4.3bn debt-service relief over 2023-2026, average coupon cut from 8% to 4%) and US$5.1bn official bilateral debt (MoU with OCC signed 28 Jan 2025, ~US$2.8bn relief; bilateral agreements targeted by June 2025). Remaining US$2.7bn owed to commercial creditors under negotiation. DSA rates Ghana at 'high risk' of debt distress. Domestic debt service of ~GH¢150.2bn due 2025-2028 (GH¢57.6bn in 2027, GH¢52.5bn in 2028); external debt service US$8.7bn over four years (US$2.5bn 2027, US$2.4bn 2028). Sinking Fund held only ~US$64,000 at 7 Jan 2025. Weighted average domestic interest rate rose to 16.2% (2024); 38% of domestic debt matures in 2025.

shortfalls_admitted.text: 2024 end-period inflation of 23.8% exceeded the 15% budget target by 8.8 ppts and the IMF 18% central target, triggering an MPCC consultation.
Primary balance (commitment) worsened to a deficit of 3.9% of GDP vs a 0.5% surplus target; overall commitment deficit 7.9% vs 4.2%.
End-December 2024 IMF QPCs/ITs (primary balance, inflation, social protection spending) and all structural benchmarks due Dec 2024/Jan 2025 'likely missed'.
Expenditure (commitment) overran target by 27.1% (GH¢59.5bn) on arrears build-up and foreign-financed capex.
Central government arrears of GH¢67.5bn (5.7% of GDP) at end-2024, excluding US$1.73bn owed to IPPs, GH¢68bn owed by ECG, GH¢32bn by COCOBOD and GH¢5.75bn by Road Fund.
MDAs committed government to contracts worth over GH¢194.3bn (16.5% of GDP), most without commencement certificates; Roads alone GH¢103.6bn.

55 bilateral-loan projects stalled after debt restructuring, with ~US$3bn undisbursed, ~US$300m unpaid IPCs and potential US$1.1bn cost overruns; would take at least 12 years under the US$250m disbursement ceiling.
Sinking Fund held only about US$64,000 (vs US$319m in 2016) and debt-service cedi account GH¢143m at 7 January 2025; no buffers built for 2027-2028 debt humps.
Energy sector financing shortfall estimated at US$2.23bn for 2025 and US$8.94bn (GH¢145.8bn) for 2023-2026; MoF paid ~US$1.5bn (GH¢20.8bn) in 2024.

Cocoa production down nearly 50% in three years; 330,000 tonnes of contracts rolled over; US$840m revenue losses plus US$495m from roll-overs; COCOBOD debt GH¢32.5bn; cocoa road contracts GH¢21bn of which only GH¢4.4bn recorded.
GH¢30.3bn spent on financial sector clean-up with 'negligible' impact; NIB situation 'dire'; GFSF Fund A1 (World Bank US$250m) not operational.
Bank of Ghana negative equity reached GH¢66.4bn at end-2023.
Agenda 111: about US$400m spent without a single hospital operationalised.
Revenue shortfalls in 2024: grants 44.9% below target, other revenue 20.8% below, taxes on domestic goods and services 9.8% below.
2024 crude oil output 48.24m barrels, 5.9% below the 51.25m barrel benchmark.
Tax refund account: of GH¢29.11bn accrued over eight years, GH¢16.6bn (57%) was misapplied.
Less than 50% of DACF releases reached District Assemblies in recent years.
SME and personal income tax compliance below 30%.
321 pharmacists employed since June 2023 have not been paid.
Ghana missed ECOWAS convergence criteria on deficit (5.2%), inflation (22.9%) and exchange rate (-19.2%).

Domestic debt refinancing risk: weighted average rate up from 13.7% to 16.2%; average time to maturity fell from 6.1 to 4.8 years; 38% of domestic debt matures in 2025; ~GH¢111.1bn of T-bills rolled weekly.
Rural Telephony: only 92 of 1,477 completed towers fully operational.
Banking sector NPL ratio rose to 21.8% in December 2024.
ABFA 2024: only GH¢7.6bn of GH¢8.0bn budget utilised; Accra-Tema Motorway ABFA line 16.8% below budget.
Many bills (e.g. Rent Bill, Social Protection Bill, Intestate Succession Bill) laid but not passed before the 8th Parliament rose.
EOCO investigated 563 cases with 15 prosecutions and no convictions.

risks: Energy sector financing shortfalls (US$2.23bn in 2025) and ECG collection inefficiencies/system losses (p31, p65)
Cocoa sector: falling output, rolled-over forward contracts, COCOBOD debt and quasi-fiscal spending (p32)
Financial sector: NIB capital gap and slow GFSF deployment; rising NPLs (p35, p59)
Heavy reliance on short-term T-bill financing and refinancing/rollover risk (p27, p50, p74)
Debt-service humps in 2027-2028 (domestic GH¢57.6bn and GH¢52.5bn; external US$2.5bn and US$2.4bn) with minimal buffers (p27)
High risk of debt distress per DSA until external restructuring completes (p50, p74)
Unvalidated arrears and off-budget commitments (GH¢194.3bn) that may crystallise (p26)
Suspension of USAID health financing creating a funding gap (p64)
Commodity price volatility (oil, gold, cocoa) and global uncertainty (p19, p20)
Illegal mining (galamsey) degrading water bodies and forests (p105, p107, p112)
Climate shocks (El Nino impact on cocoa; floods; coastal erosion) (p56, p111)
Stalled bilateral projects and IMF disbursement ceilings delaying capital projects (p28)
Exchange rate pressure: cedi depreciated a further 5.3% vs US$ in Jan-Feb 2025 (p59)
data_quality_notes: Page numbers are PDF page numbers (printed page + 12 in main text).
Fiscal framework values use Appendix 2A/3A (exact GH¢ figures re-read with PyMuPDF) where possible; text-rounded figures (e.g. non-oil tax GH¢181.6bn) used where the appendix has no matching line.
Table 38 (% of GDP, p78) is column-misaligned in text extraction; values were re-mapped row by row and cross-checked against Appendix 3A ratios.

Speech vs appendix discrepancies: DACF 7.51bn vs 7,576.2m; nursing trainee allowances 480m vs 771.0m; teacher trainee 203m vs 207.8m; net domestic financing 36.8bn vs 36,986.6m; 2024 primary expenditure 232,488 (text) vs 232,448 (table).
Accra-Kumasi by-pass completion percentages come from a garbled table (p114); lot-to-percentage mapping is best-effort.
Appendix 6 MMDA 'Grand Total' column excludes compensation; both figures given and regional amount_ghs_m sums them.

Appendix 4A internal inconsistency: listed Multi-Sectoral line items sum to GH¢192,022.5m but the stated Multi-Sectoral total is GH¢188,835.6m (difference GH¢3,187.0m = the 'Transfers for Social Protection (LEAP)' line); the stated total reconciles with the GH¢290,971.2m appropriation and Appendix 3A, so that LEAP line may be double-counted in the line items.
No explicit 2025 public debt-to-GDP target and no exchange-rate target are stated in the document.
